surf.label: Figure 1 · Scalarization and Pareto-front spacing
surf.caption: The paper’s bandit example compares points produced by uniform weights with points from geometry-aware sampling. Even spacing in weight space does not imply even spacing on the Pareto front.
surf.alt: Original SURF Figure 1: uniformly spaced weights and geometry-aware weights produce different coverage of the Pareto front.

surf.label: Figure 2 · The SURF procedure
surf.caption: SURF connects weights to arc length through a CDF. When the map is known, it is inverted directly; otherwise the method alternates between scalarized solves and CDF reconstruction.
surf.alt: Original SURF overview showing the known-CDF rule and the iterative sampling, inner-solver, and CDF-estimation rule.

birq.label: Figure 1 · Two sources of speech-learning targets
birq.caption: A shared encoder processes unmasked speech to generate enhanced targets from intermediate features through Gumbel-softmax selection. A fixed random quantizer maps raw input to anchoring targets. The masked prediction task learns from both branches, with gradients through enhanced-target generation.
birq.alt: Original BiRQ architecture: a shared speech encoder generates enhanced labels from intermediate features, alongside anchoring labels from raw input.

pbgd-free.label: Figure 1 · Single-loop update structure
pbgd-free.caption: The diagram compares the original and perturbed response updates in V-PBGD and F2SA with PBGD-Free’s single-loop update. With K = 1, PBGD-Free takes one perturbed-response step followed by one upper-variable step. The flatness analysis bounds the omitted original-response correction.
pbgd-free.alt: Original update comparison: V-PBGD and F2SA have inner refinements; PBGD-Free has one lower step followed by an upper step.

blocc.label: Figure 1 · The missing constraint contribution
blocc.caption: In the paper’s example, the value-function gradient includes a Lagrange-multiplier term. Omitting that term can reverse the descent direction. This is why the coupled constraints enter BLOCC’s primal-dual formulation.
blocc.alt: Original BLOCC Figure 1 comparing the value function with gradients computed with and without the constraint multiplier.

efficient-penalty.label: Figure 3 · Joint gradients versus reduced gradients
efficient-penalty.caption: Example 3 compares the upper partial gradient of the joint penalty objective with the reduced-objective gradient at different penalty values. Evaluating along the optimized lower response reveals the cancellation analyzed by the reduced-smoothness theorems.
efficient-penalty.alt: Original penalty-method Figure 3 comparing joint-gradient spheres and reduced-gradient lines for different penalty constants.

retailagent.label: Figure 2 · Observation, action, and self-conditioning
retailagent.caption: Numerical-text, visual, memory, and learned soft-token pathways into RetailAgent’s frozen LLM. Numerical-text histories use completed intervals. The chart and encoder branches use archived reconstructed one-minute inputs, whose provenance is documented in Appendix A.1.
retailagent.alt: RetailAgent architecture with text and vision inputs, a self-authored memory route, and a GRU-and-adapter soft-token branch connected to a frozen LLM and a long-or-flat action.
retailagent.extraction: Figure 2 cropped from PDF page 3; arXiv HTML omits this diagram.

smoothness.label: Table I · The constraint regime changes the complexity
smoothness.caption: Table I separates fixed, general coupled, and affine-in-y constraints. The complexity column combines outer iterations with the work of the lower-level solver for each regime.
smoothness.alt: Original EUSIPCO Table I comparing smoothness and total complexity across fixed, nonlinear coupled, and affine lower-level constraint regimes.
smoothness.extraction: Table I cropped from the original proceedings PDF page 2.
